title: Testing & CI/CD
tagline: Unit tests, integration tests, E2E, TDD red-green-refactor, the test pyramid, and the CI/CD pipeline — the full quality and delivery system.

sections.content:
Software that is not tested is software that is broken in ways you have not found yet. Every non-trivial codebase accumulates invisible assumptions: the belief that this function always receives a non-null argument, that the database never returns an unexpected shape, that the third-party library behaves consistently across versions. Without a disciplined testing strategy, every change is a gamble — you ship and hope. With one, a failing test is a blinking dashboard warning caught in seconds, not a 2 a.m. incident page.

**Testing** is the discipline of verifying correctness at multiple granularities. A **unit test** probes a single function or class in complete isolation, replacing every dependency with a lightweight fake. An **integration test** wires two or more real components together — a service plus a database, a router plus a handler — and verifies they collaborate correctly. An **end-to-end (E2E) test** drives the whole application from the user's perspective, clicking through a real browser or sending real HTTP requests, confirming the system behaves as a product rather than as a collection of parts. Each layer catches a different class of bug; no single layer is sufficient on its own.

**Continuous Integration (CI)** is the infrastructure that runs those tests automatically on every code change. Every push to a shared repository triggers a pipeline: lint, type-check, unit tests, integration tests, build. Failures block the change from merging. **Continuous Delivery (CD)** extends that pipeline to automatically deploy every green build to a staging environment — and in the most mature organisations, to production itself. Together, tests plus CI/CD form a quality and delivery system that lets teams ship frequently, confidently, and with minimal manual ceremony.

This chapter covers each layer of the testing hierarchy in depth, the **Test-Driven Development (TDD)** discipline of writing tests before code, the mechanics of mocking and dependency injection, code coverage as a metric, and the anatomy of a real CI/CD pipeline. By the end you will understand not just *what* each piece does, but *why* the whole system is designed the way it is.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Developer pushes code"]
  A --> B["CI: lint + type-check"]
  B --> C["CI: unit tests"]
  C --> D["CI: integration tests"]
  D --> E{"All pass?"}
  E -- No --> F["Notify developer\nblock merge"]
  E -- Yes --> G["Build artefact"]
  G --> H["CD: deploy to staging"]
  H --> I["E2E smoke tests"]
  I --> J["CD: deploy to production"]
sections.caption: The full CI/CD pipeline: every push triggers automated quality gates, and only green builds travel toward production.

sections.title: Quality Control on a Factory Assembly Line
sections.content:
Picture a car factory with a long assembly line. At the very first station, an inspector checks each individual component — a bolt is the right diameter, a spring has the correct tension rating, a circuit board passes a continuity test. These checks are **unit tests**: cheap, fast (a few seconds each), and laser-focused on one thing at a time. Because they happen early, catching a defective bolt costs almost nothing — pull it out and replace it before it touches anything else.

Further down the line, a sub-assembly — brake caliper, spring, and lever — is bolted together and stress-tested as a unit. This is the **integration test** station. The inspector is no longer checking the bolt alone; she is verifying that the bolt and the caliper and the spring all *work together* — the lever moves the correct distance, the caliper clamps with the right force. These checks take longer (real mechanical I/O), but they catch interface mismatches that the individual-component checks cannot reveal: a bolt that is dimensionally correct but too slippery for the caliper's thread pattern.

At the very end of the line sits the quality-control track: a real car, driven by a real test driver at real speed. This is the **E2E test**. It is expensive (an hour of the test driver's time, fuel, track usage) and fragile (weather affects results, the driver's mood matters). You only run it on complete cars — not every sub-assembly — and you reserve it for the critical paths: acceleration, braking, steering, airbags. You do not E2E-test the cup holder.

**TDD (Test-Driven Development)** is the discipline of writing the *inspection checklist before building the part*. The inspector writes down exactly what a passing bolt looks like, and only then does the machinist start turning metal. The checklist is the test; if it fails, the part is not done yet. This is the Red (checklist fails, part does not exist) → Green (part passes inspection) → Refactor (improve the machining process without breaking the checklist) cycle.

**CI/CD** is the automated conveyor belt: the moment a part leaves a workstation, it is placed on the belt and carried to every inspection station automatically. If it fails any station, an alarm sounds and the part is pulled. Nothing broken ever reaches the delivery truck.

sections.title: Unit Tests: The Foundation of the Pyramid
sections.content:
A **unit test** verifies a single *unit of behaviour* — typically a function or a method — in complete isolation from its dependencies. 'Isolation' is the operative word: if your function calls a database, the unit test does not use the real database. If it calls an HTTP endpoint, the test does not make a real network request. Instead, you substitute **test doubles** (mocks, stubs, or fakes) that simulate the dependency's behaviour in a controlled, deterministic way.

Why isolation? Because the moment a test depends on an external system, it inherits that system's failure modes: network timeouts, flaky DNS, a database that was not seeded correctly, a third-party API rate limit. Isolated unit tests are **deterministic** (same input → same output, always), **fast** (milliseconds, not seconds), and **focused** (when a unit test fails, you know *exactly* which function broke).

In JavaScript, **Jest** is the dominant unit-testing framework. Its structure is declarative: `describe` creates a named group of related tests, `it` (or `test`) defines a single test case with a human-readable description, and `expect` chains assertions. Jest ships with a rich assertion library (`toBe`, `toEqual`, `toThrow`, `toBeCloseTo`), a built-in mock system (`jest.fn()`, `jest.spyOn`, `jest.mock`), and a code-coverage reporter.

A well-written unit test suite has a few hallmarks:
- **Each `it` block tests exactly one behaviour** — one happy path, one edge case, or one error condition. If a test has two `expect` calls testing different behaviours, split it.
- **Tests are independent** — no shared mutable state between tests. Jest's `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks exist precisely to set up and tear down isolated state.
- **Test names read as specifications** — `it('returns 90 when a premium member buys a 100-unit item')` documents intended behaviour as clearly as a product spec.
- **Assertions are on observable outputs**, not on internal state or private methods.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Unit Test"]
  A --> B["Function / Method\nunder test"]
  B --> C["Mock DB\n(controlled fake)"]
  B --> D["Mock HTTP\n(controlled fake)"]
  B --> E["Stub Logger\n(no-op)"]
  B --> F["Assert output\nor side effect"]
sections.caption: A unit test replaces all real dependencies with test doubles, leaving only the function under test exposed to real logic.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `calculateDiscount` tests cover every branch: three member types (three happy paths), the rounding edge case, and two error conditions. The `OrderService` test replaces real HTTP with `jest.fn()` — a mock function that records calls and returns a controlled value. After calling `fetchOrder`, we assert both on the returned data AND on how the mock was called, verifying the function passes the correct URL. This is the dual-assertion pattern for testing collaborations.

sections.title: Mocks, Stubs, Spies: What Is the Difference?
sections.content:
The testing literature uses **test double** as the umbrella term for any object that stands in for a real dependency in a test. Under that umbrella live several related but distinct concepts:

**Stub**: A stub returns a pre-configured value and does nothing else. It is the simplest test double — replace a database call with `() => Promise.resolve({ id: 1 })`. Stubs exist purely to supply the function under test with the data it needs; they do not care how they are called.

**Mock**: A mock is a stub that also *records* how it was called — how many times, with what arguments, in what order. After exercising the system under test, you assert on the mock: `expect(mock.send).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)`. Mocks verify *collaboration*: not just that the function returns the right result, but that it correctly asked its dependencies to do the right thing. `jest.fn()` creates mocks in Jest.

**Spy**: A spy wraps a *real* implementation and records calls without replacing the behaviour. `jest.spyOn(emailService, 'send')` lets `send` execute normally while also tracking calls. Use spies when you want to verify that a method was called (collaboration) but still need the real side effect — or when replacing the real implementation would be too invasive.

**Fake**: A fake is a simplified but functional replacement — an in-memory database, an in-memory queue, a filesystem in RAM. Unlike stubs, fakes actually *work*; they just use a simpler implementation than the real thing. Integration tests often use fakes or real test containers rather than mocks.

**Dependency Injection (DI)** is the architectural pattern that makes all of this possible. Instead of `OrderService` creating its own `HttpClient` internally (which makes it impossible to swap for a test double), the real client is *passed in from outside* — via a constructor parameter, a function argument, or a DI container. This seam is what tests exploit to replace dependencies with doubles.

sections.title: Integration Tests: Testing the Seams
sections.content:
Unit tests verify individual functions. But two individually correct functions can still fail when connected — if function A expects its collaborator to return `{ userId: number }` but function B returns `{ user_id: string }`, the bug lives at the *seam*, not inside either function. Integration tests exist to find exactly these contract mismatches.

An integration test wires two or more real components together and verifies their collaboration. Common patterns:

**Service + database**: Start a real (or in-memory) database, seed it with test data, run the service method, and assert on the resulting database state or returned entities. Tools like **Testcontainers** spin up a real PostgreSQL or Redis in a Docker container per test run, giving you production-faithful behaviour without coupling to a shared test database.

**HTTP handler + router**: In Node/Express, use **Supertest** to send real HTTP requests to your router without binding a network port. The handler and all its middleware run, but no actual server is needed. You assert on the HTTP response status code, headers, and body.

**Queue consumer + event emitter**: Publish a real event to an in-process queue and assert that the consumer correctly processes it and produces the expected output.

Integration tests are necessarily slower than unit tests — real I/O, real query parsing, real serialisation. A test suite that takes 2 milliseconds per unit test might take 200 milliseconds per integration test. This is acceptable because you have *far fewer* integration tests. The pyramid shape is not aesthetic; it reflects the cost curve: run thousands of unit tests in 10 seconds, a few hundred integration tests in a few minutes, and a handful of E2E tests in 10-20 minutes.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Integration Test"]
  A --> B["Service layer\n(real code)"]
  B --> C["Real DB\n(test container)"]
  A --> D["Assert DB state\nor HTTP response"]
sections.caption: Integration tests use real components wired together — no mocks for the internal seams, but still isolated from production data.

sections.title: End-to-End Tests: The User's Perspective
sections.content:
**End-to-End (E2E) tests** drive the application exactly as a user would. For a web application, that means controlling a real browser (via **Playwright** or **Cypress**), navigating to pages, filling in forms, clicking buttons, and asserting on what the user sees — visible text, URL changes, toast notifications. For an API service, E2E tests send real HTTP requests to a running server (possibly against a staging environment) and assert on the full response including status codes, response bodies, and even side effects in the database or a downstream service.

The defining characteristic of E2E tests is that they exercise the **entire system stack** — the browser, the JavaScript bundle, the API layer, the service layer, the database, and any third-party integrations — without any substitutions. This gives them the highest possible confidence that the system actually works as a product.

But that confidence comes at a steep cost:

**Speed**: A Playwright test that navigates to a login page, fills in credentials, and asserts the dashboard loaded can take 3-10 seconds. A suite of 200 such tests runs for 30+ minutes. CI pipelines cannot afford this on every push.

**Brittleness**: E2E tests select UI elements by selectors — CSS classes, test IDs, ARIA labels. Any redesign that changes a class name or moves a button can break tests with zero actual regression in behaviour. The tests are sensitive to *how* things look, not just *what* they do.

**Flakiness**: Network timing, animation delays, and race conditions create intermittent failures. A test that passes 99% of the time and fails randomly is worse than no test — it trains developers to ignore red pipelines.

For these reasons, E2E tests should be reserved for **critical user journeys**: login/logout, account creation, checkout, payment confirmation. The test pyramid recommends roughly 70% unit tests, 20% integration tests, and 10% E2E tests — and in practice many teams keep fewer than 50 E2E tests total.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["E2E Test\nPlaywright / Cypress"]
  A --> B["Real Browser"]
  B --> C["Frontend Bundle"]
  C --> D["API Server"]
  D --> E["Database"]
  D --> F["Third-party APIs"]
  B --> G["Assert: page content\nURL, visibility"]
sections.caption: E2E tests traverse the entire stack — browser through database — with no substitutions, giving maximum confidence at maximum cost.

sections.title: The Test Pyramid: Ratios, Speed, and Confidence
sections.content:
The **test pyramid** (coined by Mike Cohn in *Succeeding with Agile*, 2009) is a visual prescription for how to distribute tests across the three layers. The pyramid sits on a broad base of unit tests, a smaller middle layer of integration tests, and a narrow apex of E2E tests.

The rationale is purely economic. Unit tests are cheap to write (a few lines), fast to run (milliseconds), and pinpoint failures precisely (the function name is in the test name). Integration tests cost more (infrastructure setup, slower execution) but catch a class of bugs unit tests cannot. E2E tests are the most expensive — slow, fragile, hard to maintain, requiring a running environment — but give the most realistic confidence.

A healthy ratio for a medium-sized web application: **~60-70% unit, ~20-30% integration, ~5-10% E2E**. Violating this ratio has predictable consequences. Teams with too many E2E tests — the **ice cream cone anti-pattern** (inverted pyramid) — have CI pipelines that take an hour, developers who ignore red builds because 'the tests are always flaky', and a false sense of security (many E2E tests miss business logic bugs that unit tests would catch). Teams with too few tests of any kind ship bugs constantly.

One practical heuristic: **test at the lowest level that can catch the bug**. If a pure function has a subtle edge case, a unit test catches it in milliseconds. Only escalate to integration if the bug lives at a seam between components. Only escalate to E2E if the bug is in the full user journey.

Note that the pyramid is a *guideline*, not a law. Some systems — heavy UI applications, ML pipelines, distributed systems with complex emergent behaviour — legitimately shift ratios. But the default should be pyramid-shaped until you have a clear reason to deviate.

sections.title: Test-Driven Development: Red, Green, Refactor
sections.content:
**Test-Driven Development (TDD)** is a development discipline, not a testing strategy. It reverses the conventional order: instead of writing production code and then writing tests to verify it, TDD demands that you write a **failing test first** — before a single line of production code exists.

The cycle has three phases and repeats continuously:

**Red**: Write the smallest possible test that describes a behaviour the code should have. Run it. It fails — either because the function does not exist yet, or because the existing implementation does not handle the new case. The red phase confirms your test is actually testing something. A test that passes immediately without any production code is worthless (it is testing nothing).

**Green**: Write the *minimum* production code required to make the test pass. Not the cleanest code, not the complete code — the minimum. A hardcoded return value is acceptable at this stage if it makes the test pass. This discipline forces you to focus on one behaviour at a time.

**Refactor**: Now that the test is green and you have a safety net, improve the code — extract a helper function, rename a variable for clarity, consolidate duplicate logic. Run the tests after every change. If you break a test, your refactoring introduced a regression; revert and try again. The refactor phase is where code quality actually lives.

Then repeat: add the next test. The new test should fail if the production code is not yet complete for that case (Red), then you make it pass (Green), then clean up (Refactor).

TDD's primary benefit is *design feedback*, not test coverage. When a function is hard to test — because it has too many dependencies, or it requires a specific order of operations, or it mixes business logic with I/O — the test is telling you the design is wrong. Testability and good design are strongly correlated. Functions that are easy to test tend to be small, focused, and loosely coupled. TDD surfaces this feedback during development, when it is cheap to act on, rather than after the design is baked in.

The secondary benefit is a complete, always-green test suite as a *by-product* of development. Every line of production code was written to satisfy a test. Coverage is high by construction, not by post-hoc effort.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["RED: write a failing test"]
  A --> B["RUN: test fails as expected"]
  B --> C["GREEN: write minimum code to pass"]
  C --> D["RUN: test passes"]
  D --> E["REFACTOR: improve code quality"]
  E --> F["RUN: tests still pass"]
  F --> A
sections.caption: The TDD red-green-refactor loop: tests drive design, green gives permission to refactor, and refactoring is always safe because the tests guard correctness.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Each iteration shows the full Red-Green-Refactor loop in miniature. Notice: the first Green implementation is deliberately naive (hardcoded 0). The next failing test *forces* the implementation to grow. After the third iteration, refactoring extracts `_lineTotal` for clarity — and all previous tests still pass, giving confidence the refactor did not break anything. In a real project this cycle repeats dozens of times per hour.

sections.title: Code Coverage: Metric, Not Goal
sections.content:
**Code coverage** is a measurement of how much of your production code is exercised when your test suite runs. Most coverage tools (Istanbul/nyc for JavaScript, JaCoCo for Java, Coverage.py for Python) report four dimensions:

- **Statement coverage**: what percentage of individual statements were executed
- **Branch coverage**: what percentage of decision outcomes were taken (both the `true` and `false` branches of every `if`)
- **Function coverage**: what percentage of functions were called at all
- **Line coverage**: similar to statement, but at the source-line level

**Branch coverage** is the most meaningful metric for catching logic bugs. A function with an `if/else` might have 100% line coverage if only the `if` branch executes — but the `else` branch is untested and could be wrong.

A common industry target is **80% branch coverage**. This threshold is not magical — it reflects a practical trade-off between the cost of writing tests and the marginal value of the last 20%. The final 20% is often defensive code (`catch` blocks for infrastructure errors), dead code paths that cannot be reached in practice, or trivial getters. Chasing 100% coverage tends to produce tests that test the *implementation* (asserting on internal mechanics) rather than *behaviour*, which makes the tests fragile and the codebase expensive to refactor.

Coverage thresholds can be enforced in CI. Jest's configuration supports `coverageThreshold` — if any metric falls below the threshold, the CI job fails even if all tests pass. This prevents coverage from silently eroding as new features are added without tests.

Important caveat: **100% coverage does not mean zero bugs**. Tests can execute every line and still miss the bug — if the assertion is wrong, or if the test data does not exercise the problematic edge case. Coverage tells you which code was *run*, not which code was *correctly tested*. High coverage with shallow assertions is a false sense of security.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The spy wraps `emailService.send` without replacing it — the real function still runs. After `placeOrder`, we verify that the order service sent the email with the right recipient, subject, and body. `expect.stringContaining` is a partial matcher — ideal when you care about key content but not exact string formatting. The `mockRestore` call removes the spy after the test, preventing state leakage between tests.

sections.title: CI/CD: From Commit to Production
sections.content:
**Continuous Integration (CI)** and **Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD)** are the operational infrastructure that automates the path from a developer's commit to a running service in production.

CI was originally described by Martin Fowler and Kent Beck in the context of Extreme Programming in the late 1990s. The core principle: every developer integrates their work into the shared main branch *at least once per day*, and every integration triggers an automated build and test run. This prevents the **integration hell** of long-lived feature branches — the nightmare of merging weeks of divergent work only to find hundreds of conflicts and regressions.

**What a CI pipeline does**: When a developer pushes a commit (or opens a pull request), the CI server (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Jenkins, Buildkite) clones the repository into a fresh environment, installs dependencies, and runs a sequence of jobs:

1. **Lint and type-check**: Fast static analysis catches syntax errors, type mismatches, and style violations before running any code. If lint fails, there is no point running tests.
2. **Unit tests**: Typically run in parallel across multiple workers. A project with 5,000 unit tests might shard them across 4 workers, completing in 30 seconds instead of 2 minutes.
3. **Integration tests**: Run after unit tests pass. May require spinning up Docker containers for databases, caches, or queues.
4. **Build**: Compile TypeScript, bundle the frontend, build a Docker image. The output is a versioned, deployable *artefact*.
5. **Security scan**: Tools like Snyk or Dependabot scan dependencies for known CVEs.

If any step fails, the pipeline stops, notifies the developer (Slack, email, GitHub status check), and *blocks the pull request from merging*. This is the critical enforcement mechanism: a red pipeline is not a suggestion. The main branch is always green.

**What CD adds**: Once the CI pipeline produces a green artefact, CD takes over. **Continuous Delivery** means the artefact is automatically deployed to a staging environment — a production-identical system with synthetic data — where E2E smoke tests run. The artefact is then *ready* to deploy to production, but a human approves the final promotion (a click in a dashboard). **Continuous Deployment** removes even that approval: every green build goes to production automatically. This is the model used by companies that deploy hundreds of times per day (Netflix, Amazon, Etsy).

**Environments**: A typical pipeline flows through: `dev` (developer local) → `feature` (ephemeral, per-PR) → `staging` (stable, shared, production-like) → `production`. Each environment gets the same artefact, validated at each gate. Feature flags allow code to be deployed to production but not yet activated for users — decoupling *deployment* from *release*.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Lint
  Lint --> UnitTests : pass
  Lint --> Failed : fail
  UnitTests --> IntegrationTests : pass
  UnitTests --> Failed : fail
  IntegrationTests --> Build : pass
  IntegrationTests --> Failed : fail
  Build --> StagingDeploy : artefact ok
  StagingDeploy --> E2ESmoke
  E2ESmoke --> ProdDeploy : pass
  E2ESmoke --> Failed : fail
  ProdDeploy --> [*]
  Failed --> [*]
sections.caption: CI/CD as a state machine: each stage must pass before the next begins. Any failure terminates the pipeline and blocks the release.

sections.title: CI/CD Configuration in Practice
sections.content:
Most modern CI/CD systems use **pipeline-as-code**: the pipeline is defined in a YAML file checked into the repository alongside the code. GitHub Actions uses `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; GitLab CI uses `.gitlab-ci.yml`; CircleCI uses `.circleci/config.yml`. Because the pipeline definition is versioned with the code, every branch can have a different pipeline, and changes to the CI configuration go through the same review process as code changes.

A GitHub Actions workflow file declares:
- **Triggers** (`on:`) — which events start the pipeline: `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule` (cron), `workflow_dispatch` (manual)
- **Jobs** — independent units of work that can run in parallel or sequentially (`needs:` declares dependencies)
- **Steps** — sequential commands within a job: `uses:` to run a reusable Action (e.g. `actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-node`), `run:` to execute shell commands
- **Environment variables and secrets** — secrets are stored encrypted in the repository settings and injected at runtime, never visible in logs

A key design principle: **jobs should be idempotent and stateless**. Each job starts from a clean environment (a fresh container or VM). State that needs to persist between jobs (the built artefact, test coverage reports) is transferred via **artefact upload/download** steps, not shared filesystem state.

**Branch protection rules** are the enforcement mechanism. In GitHub, you configure the `main` branch to require: (1) all CI jobs pass, (2) at least one approval, (3) the branch is up to date with main before merging. This creates a hard gate: broken code literally cannot merge.

**Deployment strategies** in the CD phase control how the new artefact replaces the old one:
- **Blue/green**: Two identical environments; traffic switches from blue (current) to green (new) instantly. Rollback is instant (switch back).
- **Canary**: The new version receives 1-5% of traffic initially. Metrics are monitored; if error rates stay low, traffic gradually shifts to 100%. If errors spike, traffic reverts.
- **Rolling update**: Kubernetes-style; old pods are replaced one by one. Zero downtime but the old and new versions coexist briefly.

**A brief history of the ideas**: TDD was popularised by Kent Beck in his book *Test-Driven Development: By Example* (2002), though similar ideas appeared in Smalltalk communities in the 1980s. The Test Pyramid was coined by Mike Cohn in 2009. The term 'CI' was formalised by Martin Fowler and Matthew Foemmel in a 1997 paper. GitHub Actions launched in 2019 and rapidly displaced Jenkins and Travis CI as the default for open-source projects. Playwright (Microsoft) launched in 2020 and has largely replaced Selenium and early Cypress for modern E2E testing, offering faster execution, native async support, and better multi-browser coverage out of the box.

**Common mistakes and interview insights to know cold:**

- **'Test implementation, not behaviour'** is the most common unit-testing mistake. If your test breaks whenever you rename a private method, it is testing implementation. Tests should assert on public inputs and outputs; internals should be free to change.
- **Shared mutable state between tests** causes flaky, order-dependent suites. Use `beforeEach` to reset state; never rely on one test setting up data that another test consumes.
- **Over-mocking** produces a test suite that passes even when the code is completely wrong — because every dependency is mocked, nothing real ever runs. Prefer integration tests for code with complex dependency interactions.
- **Testing the happy path only** is the most common omission. Interviewers often ask: 'What happens if the input is null? What happens if the network fails?' Always test error paths and edge cases.
- **CI as a safety net, not a replacement for local testing**: Pushing broken code and waiting for CI feedback is a bad habit — it blocks your own pipeline and wastes shared resources. Run tests locally before pushing.
- **Interview framing**: When asked about testing strategy, structure your answer around the pyramid: unit tests for logic, integration tests for seams, E2E for critical paths. Mention TDD and when you would apply it (new functions, bug fixes). Mention mocking and why it matters for isolation.

items: The **test pyramid** prescribes many fast unit tests (~70%), fewer integration tests (~20%), and very few slow E2E tests (~10%) — this ratio maximises bug-catching ability while keeping CI pipelines fast and reliable.
**Unit tests** isolate a single function from all dependencies using test doubles (mocks, stubs, spies), producing millisecond-fast, deterministic results that pinpoint failures precisely.
**Integration tests** wire real components together (service + database, router + handler) to catch contract mismatches at seams that mocks cannot reveal.
**E2E tests** drive the full application stack from the user's perspective — highest confidence, highest cost; reserve them for critical user journeys like login and checkout.

**TDD (red-green-refactor)** writes a failing test first, then the minimum code to make it pass, then refactors under the safety net — this forces testable design and produces a complete test suite as a development by-product.

**Code coverage** (aim for 80%+ branch coverage) is a useful floor metric, not a goal — 100% coverage with shallow assertions is a false sense of security; test critical paths and edge cases, not every line.

**CI/CD pipelines** run lint, tests, and build on every push, block merges on failure, automatically deploy green builds to staging, and (in full CD) to production — enabling teams to ship frequently and confidently.

quiz.question: In the test pyramid, which layer should have the most tests and why?
options: E2E tests — they provide the highest confidence.
Integration tests — they catch seam-level bugs.
Unit tests — they are the fastest, cheapest, and most precise.
Manual tests — they are the most realistic.
quiz.explanation: Unit tests form the broad base of the pyramid because they run in milliseconds, require no external infrastructure, and pinpoint failures to a single function. E2E tests sit at the narrow apex — fewest, slowest, most realistic. More E2E tests than unit tests is the 'ice cream cone' anti-pattern.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of the TDD cycle?
options: Write code → write test → refactor
Write failing test → make it pass → refactor
Refactor → write test → make it pass
Write test → refactor → make it pass
quiz.explanation: Red (write a failing test first) → Green (write the minimum production code to make it pass) → Refactor (improve code without breaking tests). Writing the test first is the defining characteristic of TDD — it drives design and produces tests as a by-product of development.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a mock and a spy in unit testing?
options: Mocks run the real implementation; spies replace it.
Mocks replace the implementation with a controlled fake and record calls; spies wrap the real implementation to record calls without replacing it.
Mocks are only for HTTP calls; spies are for database calls.
Spies are used in integration tests; mocks are only for unit tests.
quiz.explanation: A mock (e.g. `jest.fn()`) replaces the real function entirely with a controlled fake that returns a preset value and records how it was called. A spy (e.g. `jest.spyOn`) wraps the real implementation — the real code still executes — but also tracks calls so you can assert on them afterward.

quiz.question: Why are integration tests slower than unit tests?
options: Integration tests use mocks, which are slower than real code.
Integration tests wire real components together, including real I/O like database queries and HTTP calls.
Integration tests run in a browser, which is inherently slow.
Integration tests are written by separate QA teams who are less efficient.
quiz.explanation: Integration tests use real implementations of multiple components — including real database queries, real serialisation, and real network calls within the system. This I/O takes 100x or more longer than the in-memory operations of isolated unit tests. Frameworks like Testcontainers spin up real databases in Docker for each test run.

quiz.question: What does 'branch coverage' measure that 'line coverage' does not?
options: Whether every function was called at least once.
Whether both the true and false outcomes of every conditional were exercised.
Whether the code was compiled without errors.
Whether the test ran within the time limit.
quiz.explanation: Branch coverage checks that both sides of every `if/else`, ternary, and switch case were exercised by tests. Line coverage only requires that a line was executed — it can miss the `else` branch entirely. Branch coverage is more meaningful for catching logic bugs in conditional paths.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of blocking pull requests when CI tests fail?
options: To automatically fix failing tests.
To enforce that the main branch is always in a deployable, green state.
To prevent developers from pushing on Fridays.
To generate test coverage reports automatically.
quiz.explanation: Blocking merges on test failure enforces the invariant that the main branch is always green (passing). This is the foundation of continuous delivery — if main is always deployable, you can ship from it at any moment without extra verification ceremonies.

quiz.question: What distinguishes Continuous Deployment from Continuous Delivery?
options: Continuous Deployment requires more unit tests than Continuous Delivery.
Continuous Delivery deploys to staging automatically; Continuous Deployment also deploys to production automatically without human approval.
Continuous Deployment uses Docker; Continuous Delivery uses virtual machines.
Continuous Delivery requires feature flags; Continuous Deployment does not.
quiz.explanation: Both automatically deploy to staging. Continuous Delivery stops there — a human approves the final production promotion. Continuous Deployment removes even that gate: every green build goes to production automatically. Companies deploying hundreds of times per day (Netflix, Amazon) use full Continuous Deployment.

quiz.question: Why are E2E tests considered 'brittle' compared to unit tests?
options: E2E tests cannot test authentication or payments.
E2E tests select UI elements by selectors that break when the UI is redesigned, even when the underlying behaviour is unchanged.
E2E tests require mocking all external services, which is fragile.
E2E tests only work on Chrome and break on other browsers.
quiz.explanation: E2E tests typically select DOM elements by CSS classes, data attributes, or ARIA labels. A UI redesign that renames a CSS class or moves a button can break dozens of tests with zero actual regression in product behaviour. This fragility is the main reason E2E suites should be kept small and focused on critical paths.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of Dependency Injection (DI) in the context of testing?
options: It allows tests to run faster by caching database connections.
It creates a seam where test doubles can be substituted for real dependencies, enabling isolation.
It automatically generates mock data for test cases.
It ensures tests run in the correct order when dependencies exist between them.
quiz.explanation: Dependency Injection passes collaborators in from outside (constructor, function parameter, DI container) rather than having the object create them internally. This seam is exactly what tests exploit — in a test, you inject a mock instead of the real implementation, achieving isolation. DI and testability are deeply coupled design concerns.

quiz.question: Which deployment strategy gradually shifts a small percentage of production traffic to the new version before full rollout?
options: Blue/green deployment
Rolling update
Canary deployment
Big-bang deployment
quiz.explanation: Canary deployment initially routes a small slice of traffic (1-5%) to the new version, monitors error rates and latency, and gradually increases the percentage if metrics stay healthy. If problems appear, traffic reverts. Blue/green switches all traffic at once. Rolling updates replace instances one by one. Canary offers the most gradual, measurable rollout.
